shortExplanation: The 13 coins consist of seven pennies and six nickels.
detailedSteps: If $n$ is the nickel count, there are $n+1$ pennies. Thus $2n+1=13$, giving six nickels and seven pennies.
The value is $6\cdot5+7=37$ cents.
commonMistakes: Adding the hypothetical extra nickel to the final value.
difficultyNotes: The extra nickel describes a comparison, not an actual coin.

shortExplanation: The factor two cancels between numerator and denominator.
commonMistakes: Adding exponents rather than subtracting a negative exponent.
difficultyNotes: A negative exponent represents a reciprocal.

shortExplanation: The 20 pavement miles are seven-fifteenths of the trip.
detailedSteps: If total length is L, the other road portions occupy $(1/3+1/5)L=8L/15$. Thus $7L/15=20$, giving $L=300/7$.
keyIdeas: The fraction of the trip on pavement
commonMistakes: Treating the remaining one-fifth as a fifth of the already remaining distance.
difficultyNotes: Both fractions refer to the whole trip.

shortExplanation: The doubled first purchase forces 6 muffin prices equal 10 banana prices.
detailedSteps: With muffin price m and banana price b, $2m+16b=2(4m+3b)$. Rearranging gives $10b=6m$, so $m/b=5/3$.
commonMistakes: Doubling the quantities instead of comparing the stated costs.
difficultyNotes: The requested ratio is muffin price divided by banana price.

shortExplanation: There are five vertical border widths and three horizontal ones.
detailedSteps: Let each pane width be w and height $5w/2$. The source has four columns and two rows, with 2-inch borders throughout.
The window width is $4w+10$, while its height is $5w+6$. Equality gives $w=4$ and window side $26$.
commonMistakes: Counting only the internal dividers and omitting the outer frame.
difficultyNotes: Use separate divider counts in the two directions.

shortExplanation: A pair costs five-thirds of one regular balloon price.
detailedSteps: In units of regular price, each pair costs $1+2/3=5/3$. A budget 30 buys 18 pairs, totaling 36 balloons.
To buy 37 would require 18 discounted pairs and one full-price balloon, costing 31; it is impossible. Larger counts cost still more.
keyIdeas: Buying discounted pairs under a fixed budget
commonMistakes: Reading one-third off as a discounted price of one-third.
difficultyNotes: Each discounted balloon requires a matched regular-price purchase.

shortExplanation: Divide the increase by B, the comparison base.
detailedSteps: The defining equation is $A=B(1+x/100)$. Solving gives $x=100(A-B)/B$.
keyIdeas: Percentage increase relative to the old value
commonMistakes: Dividing by the new value A.
difficultyNotes: The percentage increase over B uses B as its denominator.

shortExplanation: Three minutes is 180 seconds and each yard is three feet.
detailedSteps: The speed is $b/(6t)$ feet per second. In 180 seconds the distance is $30b/t$ feet, or $10b/t$ yards.
commonMistakes: Using bfeet rather than b/6 feet per interval.
difficultyNotes: Convert both the time and the distance units.

shortExplanation: The denominator has the opposite sign from w-z.
detailedSteps: The defined expression requires nonzero w,zand w≠z. Multiplying its numerator and denominator by wzgives $(w+z)/(z-w)=2014$.
Changing the denominator to w-znegates the quotient, giving−2014.
keyIdeas: Multiplying a reciprocal ratio by wz
commonMistakes: Missing the denominator reversal.
difficultyNotes: The domain permits clearing the common reciprocal factor.

shortExplanation: All carries vanish and Cmust be zero.
detailedSteps: Let the carries from the units through thousands be $u,v,w,t$. Units give $A+B=D+10u$, while tens give $C+u=10v$. Thus either $C=0,u=v=0$, or $C=9,u=v=1$.
Hundreds give $A+B+v=D+10w$. Subtracting the units equation gives $10u+v=10w$, ruling out the second branch. Hence $C=u=v=w=0$; the thousands column then forces $t=0$.
The leading column gives D=A+B≤9. Aand Bare distinct positive digits, so every D 3 through 9 is achievable by A 1,B=D−1(or A 2,B 1 for D 3), while 0,1,2 are impossible. There are seven values.
keyIdeas: A column addition with distinct digits
commonMistakes: Allowing equal Aand Bor leading zero digits.
difficultyNotes: The tens and hundreds carries together rule out the nonzero-Cbranch.

shortExplanation: The strongest listed discount is 28.75 percent.
detailedSteps: The retained fractions are $0.85^2=0.7225$, $0.9^3=0.729$, and $0.75\cdot0.95=0.7125$. The last is lowest, equivalent to 28.75 percent off.
A strictly more advantageous integer discount must exceed 28.75 percent; the smallest is 29.
commonMistakes: Adding successive percentage discounts.
difficultyNotes: The discount applies to the already reduced price.

shortExplanation: The fifth-smallest divisor is 8.
detailedSteps: For N 2014000000, the smallest divisors are 1,2,4,5,8:3 and 6 do not divide N, and 7 does not either. The powers of 2 and 5 present guarantee 4,5,8.
The map d↦N/d reverses divisor order. Therefore the fifth-largest is $N/8=251750000$.
commonMistakes: Listing large divisors directly without preserving order.
difficultyNotes: Reciprocal divisor pairing turns a large-number search into a small one.

shortExplanation: The vertical base BCis 2 sqrt(3)and its altitude from Ais 3.
detailedSteps: Use a flat-topped unit hexagon centered at the origin, with vertices $(\pm1,0)$ and $(\pm1/2,\pm\sqrt3/2)$. Reading the indicated surrounding vertices gives $A=(-2,0),B=(1,\sqrt3),C=(1,-\sqrt3)$.
Thus $BC=2\sqrt3$ and its perpendicular distance from Ais 3, so area $\tfrac12(2\sqrt3)3=3\sqrt3$.
commonMistakes: Using adjacent hexagon centers in place of the labeled vertices.
difficultyNotes: The source base runs through the right vertex of the center hexagon.

shortExplanation: The first and last digits differ by five.
detailedSteps: The positive distance driven is $99(c-a)$ and also 55 times a positive integer hour count h. Therefore $9(c-a)=5h$, so c-a is a positive multiple of 5.
Digit bounds force $c-a=5$. Then $2a+b+5\le7$, with $a\ge1,b\ge0$, gives $a=1,b=0,c=6$.
The requested sum is $1^2+0^2+6^2=37$.
commonMistakes: Ignoring that the odometer must increase during the trip.
difficultyNotes: The distance condition supplies divisibility, not an approximation.

shortExplanation: If the rectangle height is $h$, then $EF=2h/\sqrt3$.
detailedSteps: Put $D=(0,0),C=(2h,0),A=(0,h),B=(2h,h)$. The trisection rays make angles $60^\circ,30^\circ$ with $DC$, meeting $AB$ at horizontal coordinates $h/\sqrt3,h\sqrt3$.
Hence $EF=2h/\sqrt3$ and triangle area $h^2/\sqrt3$. Rectangle area is 2 h², so the ratio is $1/(2\sqrt3)=\sqrt3/6$.
commonMistakes: Using the triangle slanted sides as its altitude.
difficultyNotes: The source shows Eon the steeper ray and Fon the shallower ray.

shortExplanation: The favorable outcome count is 120+6.
detailedSteps: Exactly three equal dice can choose the repeated value in 6 ways, the differing die in 4 ways, and its different value in 5 ways, giving 120.
All four equal add 6 outcomes. Out of $6^4=1296$ equally likely outcomes, the probability is $126/1296=7/72$.
keyIdeas: Exactly three equal dice or all four equal
commonMistakes: Counting four-equal outcomes once for each triple of die positions.
difficultyNotes: Keep the exactly-three and exactly-four cases disjoint.

shortExplanation: Factoring 2 to power 1002 leaves a factor divisible by 8 but not 16.
detailedSteps: Thus $5^{1002}-1\equiv8\pmod{16}$, with exactly three factors of 2. The greatest power dividing the expression is $2^{1005}$.
keyIdeas: The exact two-adic power in a difference
commonMistakes: Assuming the visible common power 2 to 1002 is already maximal.
difficultyNotes: A residue 8 mod 16 proves both divisibility by 8 and nondivisibility by 16.

shortExplanation: Minimizing the first ten entries leaves at most 35 for the last.
detailedSteps: Sort the list, so its sixth entry is 9 and total is 110. If 8 appears k times, then 2≤k≤5 and every other value appears at mostk−1 times. All 8 s belong among the first five.

For k 2,3,4,5 the minimum first-five sums are 22,26,33,40, respectively: lists 1,2,3,8,8;1,1,8,8,8;1,8,8,8,8; and 8,8,8,8,8. The next five entries, each at least 9 with repetition capk−1, have minimum sums 55,49,47,46.
Therefore the first ten sum at least 77,75,80,86 in the four cases. The global lower bound 75 gives largest entry at most 35.
The list $1,1,8,8,8,9,9,10,10,11,35$ has total 110, median 9, and unique mode 8, attaining 35.
keyIdeas: A unique-mode constraint on an extremal list
commonMistakes: Minimizing all entries independently while accidentally creating another equally frequent mode.
difficultyNotes: The unique-mode condition is a strict frequency comparison.

shortExplanation: The smaller central angle must be at least 120 degrees.
detailedSteps: For minor central angle θ∈[0,π], the chord distance from the common center is $2\cos(\theta/2)$. It meets the radius 1 circle when this is at most 1, meaning θ≥2π/3.
The folded minor angle is uniform on[0,π], so the probability is $(\pi-2\pi/3)/\pi=1/3$. Tangency has probability zero.
keyIdeas: The central angle for a chord meeting an inner circle
commonMistakes: Using a uniformly random chord model unrelated to independently chosen endpoints.
difficultyNotes: Rotational symmetry allows fixing the first endpoint.

shortExplanation: The squared integer lies strictly between 1 and 50.
detailedSteps: $x^4-51x^2+50=(x^2-1)(x^2-50)$ is negative exactly when 1<x²<50.
The positive integer choices are 2 through 7, and their negatives also work, giving 12 integers.
commonMistakes: Includingx=±1,where the expression is zero.
difficultyNotes: Factoring in x²reduces the degree immediately.

shortExplanation: The shorter diagonal has squared length 625.
detailedSteps: Choose $A=(0,0),B=(33,0),D=(u,h),C=(u+21,h)$, with AD 10 and BC 14. Acute base angles ensure 0<u<12.
The leg equations are $u^2+h^2=100$ and $(12-u)^2+h^2=196$. Subtracting gives 144−24 u 96, so u 2,h²96.
Then $AC^2=23^2+96=625$ and $BD^2=31^2+96=1057$. The shorter diagonal is 25. Interchanging the leg assignments merely exchanges the two diagonals.
commonMistakes: Assigning the full base difference 12 to one leg projection.
difficultyNotes: The base difference splits into the two leg projections.

shortExplanation: The center distance to each radius-half semicircle is sqrt(5)/2.
detailedSteps: In the 2-by 2 square, each semicircle has radius 1/2. Equidistance from the two bottom centers fixes the required circle center x 1, and the corresponding side centers fix y 1.
The distance from(1,1)to(1/2,0)is $\sqrt{1+1/4}=\sqrt5/2$. External tangency gives $r+1/2=\sqrt5/2$, hence $r=(\sqrt5-1)/2$.
keyIdeas: External tangency to eight inward semicircles
commonMistakes: Subtracting the radius from the corner-to-center distance instead of a semicircle-center distance.
difficultyNotes: The figure identifies a circle in the central uncovered region.

shortExplanation: The two base radii multiply to the squared sphere radius.
detailedSteps: Let the sphere radius be R, bottom base radius b,and top base radius t. The frustum height is 2 R. Its axial cross-section is an isosceles trapezoid with an incircle, so opposite-side length sums agree: each slant side has length b+t.
The slant right triangle gives $(b+t)^2=(b-t)^2+(2R)^2$, hence bt=R².
The frustum volume is $(2\pi R/3)(b^2+bt+t^2)$, while twice the sphere volume is $8\pi R^3/3$. Hence $b^2+bt+t^2=4bt$, or $b^2+t^2=3bt$.
For k=b/t>1, $k^2-3k+1=0$. The larger root is $(3+\sqrt5)/2$.
keyIdeas: An inscribed sphere in a cone frustum
commonMistakes: Assuming the frustum is a cylinder or using the entire untruncated cone volume.
difficultyNotes: Tangency in the axial cross-section connects the three radii.

shortExplanation: Only two of the twelve dihedral arrangements fail.
detailedSteps: Fix 1 as the first entry and identify the two directions around the circle. A canonical representative has its second entry smaller than its last; this leaves 4!/2=12 arrangements.

All 1 through 5 are singleton sums,15 is the whole circle, and 10 through 14 are complements of singletons. Complementary consecutive blocks also pair 6 with 9 and 7 with 8. Hence the full condition is equivalent to having both consecutive sums 6 and 7.

The representatives 12345,12354,12435,12453,12534,12543,13245,13254,13425,13524,14235,14325 exhaust the 12 classes. Checking consecutive blocks, only 12534 lacks 6 and only 13245 lacks 7; every other representative has both. Thus two are bad.
commonMistakes: Treating a consecutive subset as a nonconsecutive arbitrary subset.
difficultyNotes: Complement sums reduce 15 target checks to just two.

shortExplanation: Successive probability increments are reciprocals of binomial coefficients.
detailedSteps: Let p_n be the escape probability starting at pad n. Then p 0=0,p 10=1, and for 1≤n≤9, $p_n=(n/10)p_{n-1}+((10-n)/10)p_{n+1}$.
Put $d_n=p_n-p_{n-1}$. Rearrangement gives $d_{n+1}=n\,d_n/(10-n)$. Therefore $d_k=d_1/\binom9{k-1}$ for 1≤k≤10.

Thus the starting probability p 1=d 1=63/146. The recurrence solution is unique: the difference of two solutions has zero endpoints and cannot have a nonzero interior extremum under strictly positive transition weights.
keyIdeas: Absorption probabilities with unequal step biases
commonMistakes: Using the fair random-walk probability 1/10 when the step probabilities depend on location.
difficultyNotes: The step probabilities vary with n, so equal probability increments do not apply.
